start.title: Start here: your CI/CD & GitOps path
start.description: You can build an image (Docker), run it (Kubernetes), package it (Helm), and create the ground it runs on (Terraform). This course joins them: every change…
start.html:
You can build an image (Docker), run it (Kubernetes), package it (Helm), and create the ground it runs on (Terraform). This course joins them: every change you push is tested, built, and deployed automatically, and git always says what is running.

The big idea
A pipeline checks and packages every change. GitOps then deploys whatever git says should run, and keeps the cluster that way.

Before starting: know what an image, a Deployment, and a git commit are. The Docker and Kubernetes courses cover the first two. No installation is needed until the final stage.

1 · Meet the pipeline · lessons 1–3Explain CI, CD, and GitOps, and where each tool from the other courses fits.
2 · Continuous integration · lessons 4–7Read a GitHub Actions workflow, run test → build → scan → push in the simulator, tag images safely, and keep secrets out of logs.
3 · GitOps delivery · lessons 8–11Let Argo CD deploy from git, split app and config, watch it undo hand-made changes, and roll back with git revert.
4 · Use it for real · lessons 12–14Learn team rules, then run the whole loop with your own GitHub repository and a local cluster.

Use Explore CI/CD for free practice at any time. Your progress here is saved separately from the other topics.

why.title: Why automate: from “works on my laptop” to every commit tested
why.description: Friday evening. You build the 🍕 image on your laptop, push it, and run kubectl apply by hand. It works for you. On Monday nobody knows which code is in…
why.html:
The problem
Friday evening. You build the 🍕 image on your laptop, push it, and run kubectl apply by hand. It works for you. On Monday nobody knows which code is in production, a test you forgot to run is failing, and the person who knows the deploy steps is on holiday.
The big idea
Let a machine do the same careful steps for every change: test it, build it, check it, and deploy it. People review the change; the pipeline does the repetitive work the same way every time.
WordMeaning
CI (continuous integration)Every change is merged often and checked automatically: tests, build, scans.
CD (continuous delivery or deployment)Every change that passes can be released. Delivery: ready to release with one approval. Deployment: released automatically.
PipelineThe ordered list of automatic steps a change goes through.
GitOpsGit holds the desired state of the cluster. A tool in the cluster keeps reality matching git.
Think of it like…
A pizza kitchen line. Every pizza passes the same stations: dough, toppings, oven, quality check. Nobody skips the oven on a busy night, and a burnt pizza never reaches the table.
Remember
  • CI checks every change automatically.
  • CD makes passing changes ready to release, or releases them.
  • GitOps: git says what should run; the cluster follows.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of a CI pipeline?
options: Every change gets the same checks, every time
Developers no longer need to write tests
quiz.why: The pipeline removes forgotten steps and “works on my machine” surprises.

quiz.q: In GitOps, where is the desired state of the cluster written?
quiz.why: Git is the source of truth; the cluster is kept matching it.

bridge.title: Where each tool fits in the pipeline
bridge.description: Every course you have taken becomes one station in the pipeline. 💬 commit → 🧪 test → 🐳 build image → 🔍 scan → 📦 push to registry → 🗂️ new tag in git →…
bridge.html:
Every course you have taken becomes one station in the pipeline.

💬 commit→🧪 test→🐳 build image→🔍 scan→📦 push to registry→🗂️ new tag in git→🐙 Argo CD syncs→☸️ pods update
StationToolFrom which course
Build the imageDocker (inside GitHub Actions)Docker & Compose
Describe what runsKubernetes YAML, Kustomize, or a Helm chartKubernetes, Helm
Deploy and keep it runningArgo CD in the cluster, then Kubernetes controllersKubernetes
The cluster, registry, and network themselvesTerraform, usually in its own pipelineTerraform
The big idea
CI ends when a tested image is in the registry and its tag is written to git. GitOps starts there: Argo CD notices the change in git and deploys it.

Push versus pull. A classic pipeline pushes to the cluster with kubectl and needs cluster credentials. With GitOps, Argo CD runs inside the cluster and pulls from git, so CI never needs a key to production.

Remember
  • CI produces a tested image and a new tag in git.
  • Argo CD pulls from git and deploys; CI needs no cluster credentials.
  • Terraform builds the cluster; this pipeline deploys apps onto it.

quiz.q: Which step ends CI and hands over to GitOps?
options: Writing the new image tag to git
quiz.why: Once git has the new tag, Argo CD takes over.

quiz.q: Why is pull-based GitOps safer than a pipeline running kubectl against production?
options: CI never needs production cluster credentials
quiz.why: The agent inside the cluster pulls changes, so no outside system holds a key to it.

workflow.title: Read a workflow: triggers, jobs, steps
workflow.description: GitHub Actions reads YAML files in.github/workflows/. Each file is a workflow. Part What it means on: Triggers: when to run. For example on every pull…
workflow.html:
GitHub Actions reads YAML files in .github/workflows/. Each file is a workflow.

PartWhat it means
on:Triggers: when to run. For example on every pull request, and on pushes to main.
jobs:Separate pieces of work. Each job runs on a fresh virtual machine, a runner.
needs:Order: build waits for test, and is skipped if test fails.
steps:Commands or reusable actions run one after another inside a job.
uses:A ready-made action, such as actions/checkout, which downloads your code onto the runner.
permissions:What the job’s automatic token may do. Give each job only what it needs.
📄 .github/workflows/ci.yaml · the course pipeline
# Test every pull request. On main: build, scan, push, then point deploy/ at the new image.
name: ci

on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    # A commit that only changes deploy/ (a promotion or a rollback) needs no new build.
    paths-ignore:
      - "deploy/**"
      - "argocd/**"

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.13"
      - name: Run unit tests
        working-directory: app
        run: python -m unittest -v

  build:
    needs: test
    if: github.event_name == 'push'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write
    outputs:
      image: ${{ steps.name.outputs.image }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Choose the image name (registry names must be lowercase)
        id: name
        run: echo "image=ghcr.io/${GITHUB_REPOSITORY,,}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
      - name: Build, tagged with the commit SHA
        run: docker build --build-arg APP_VERSION="$GITHUB_SHA" -t "${{ steps.name.outputs.image }}:$GITHUB_SHA" app
      - name: Scan for known vulnerabilities (fails on fixable HIGH or CRITICAL)
        run: >-
          docker run --rm -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock aquasec/trivy:0.58.1
          image --exit-code 1 --ignore-unfixed --severity HIGH,CRITICAL
          "${{ steps.name.outputs.image }}:$GITHUB_SHA"
      - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
        run: echo "${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}" | docker login ghcr.io -u "$GITHUB_ACTOR" --password-stdin
      - name: Push
        run: docker push "${{ steps.name.outputs.image }}:$GITHUB_SHA"

  promote:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Commit the new image tag to deploy/ (Argo CD deploys it)
        env:
          IMAGE: ${{ needs.build.outputs.image }}
        run: |
          sed -i "s|newName: .*|newName: $IMAGE|; s|newTag: .*|newTag: $GITHUB_SHA|" deploy/kustomization.yaml
          git config user.name "github-actions[bot]"
          git config user.email "41898282+github-actions[bot]@users.noreply.github.com"
          git commit -am "deploy: pizza $GITHUB_SHA"
          git pull --rebase origin main
          git push
The big idea
Read it as a story: on a pull request, only test. On main, test, then build, scan, and push the image, then commit the new tag so Argo CD can deploy it.

Why if: github.event_name == 'push'? Pull requests should be checked, but only merged code should become an image that can reach the cluster.

Remember
  • on = when, jobs = what, needs = order, steps = how.
  • Each job starts on a clean runner; nothing is left over from your laptop.
  • A failed job stops every job that needs it.

quiz.q: The build job has needs: test. The tests fail. What happens to build?
quiz.why: needs makes build wait for test and skip if test fails.

quiz.q: Where does GitHub look for workflow files?
quiz.why: Any YAML file in .github/workflows/ is a workflow.

pipeline.title: Test → build → scan → push
pipeline.description: A teammate pushes a change on a busy afternoon. Nobody ran the tests, and the new image contains a library with a known security hole. Which step should…
pipeline.html:
The problem
A teammate pushes a change on a busy afternoon. Nobody ran the tests, and the new image contains a library with a known security hole. Which step should have stopped it?
JobQuestion it answersIf it fails
🧪 testDoes the code still do what we expect?Nothing is built; the change is blocked.
🐳 buildCan we package it into an image?Nothing to scan or ship.
🔍 scanDoes the image contain known, fixable vulnerabilities?The image is never pushed.
📦 pushStore the image in a registry, tagged with the commit.Argo CD has nothing new to deploy.
🗂️ promoteWrite the new tag into git for Argo CD.The cluster keeps running the previous version.
The big idea
Each job is a gate. A red gate stops everything after it, so a broken or risky change never reaches the cluster. The working version keeps running.

Practice safely in the browser

A green pipeline only proves what your tests and scans check. Write tests for the things that would hurt most if they broke.
Remember
  • test → build → scan → push → promote, in that order.
  • Any red job stops the rest; production keeps the last good version.
  • Scans catch known problems, not every problem.

quiz.q: The test job fails. Does a new image reach the registry?
quiz.why: build, scan, and push all depend on test, so they are skipped.

quiz.q: The scan finds a fixable HIGH vulnerability in the base image. What is a good fix?
options: Update or slim the base image and push again
quiz.why: Fix the image; keep the gate.

tags.title: Image tags you can trust
tags.description: Production runs pizza:latest. A pod restarts on a new node and downloads latest again, but someone pushed a different image under that name an hour ago. Now…
tags.html:
The problem
Production runs pizza:latest. A pod restarts on a new node and downloads latest again, but someone pushed a different image under that name an hour ago. Now two pods run two different versions, and nobody can tell which.
The big idea
Tag every image with the commit SHA that built it. A tag like pizza:3f9c2a1 always means exactly one build of exactly one commit, so you can trace, repeat, and roll back any deploy.
Tag styleGood forProblem
latestQuick local testsChanges under your feet; impossible to roll back to
v1.4.2Human-friendly releasesCan be overwritten unless your registry blocks it
3f9c2a1… (commit SHA)Automatic pipelinesNot pretty, but always unique and traceable

The course pipeline pushes to GitHub Container Registry (ghcr.io/owner/repo:SHA) using the workflow’s automatic token, so no password is stored anywhere.

Even stronger: digests

A digest like pizza@sha256:ab12… is a fingerprint of the image content itself and can never point to anything else. Some teams deploy by digest for the strongest guarantee.

Remember
  • Never deploy latest.
  • Tag images with the commit SHA so every deploy is traceable.
  • Digests are fingerprints that can never change.

quiz.q: Why is latest risky in production?
options: It can point to a different image tomorrow
quiz.why: Mutable tags make deploys unrepeatable and rollbacks unclear.

quiz.q: What does tagging with the commit SHA give you?
options: A direct link from the running image to the exact code
quiz.why: You can always answer “which code is running?”.

secrets.title: Secrets in pipelines
secrets.description: To deploy, someone pastes a cloud access key into the workflow file. The repository is public. Within minutes, bots find the key and start expensive…
secrets.html:
The problem
To deploy, someone pastes a cloud access key into the workflow file. The repository is public. Within minutes, bots find the key and start expensive servers.
The big idea
Never write secrets in files. Store them as encrypted repository secrets, give each job the smallest permissions it needs, and prefer short-lived tokens over long-lived keys.
NeedBest option
Push images to ghcr.io from this repositoryThe automatic GITHUB_TOKEN with packages: write. Nothing to store.
Log in to a cloud (AWS, Azure, Google)OIDC: the cloud trusts a short-lived token GitHub creates for this repository. No stored key.
A third-party API keyA repository or environment secret, read as secrets.NAME in the workflow

GitHub hides secret values in logs, but a step can still leak one if it writes the value in a different form. Never print secrets, even for debugging.

Workflows from forks do not receive your secrets, by design. Do not work around this with the pull_request_target trigger unless you understand the risk: it can run untrusted code with your secrets.
Remember
  • No secrets in files; use repository or environment secrets.
  • Give each job only the permissions it needs.
  • Prefer OIDC to long-lived cloud keys.

quiz.q: What is the safest way for a workflow to log in to AWS?
options: OIDC with a role that trusts this repository
An access key pasted into ci.yaml
quiz.why: OIDC gives short-lived credentials; nothing long-lived can leak.

quiz.q: The course pipeline pushes to ghcr.io. Which credential does it use?
quiz.why: With packages: write, the built-in token can push to the repository’s registry.

gitops.title: GitOps: git is the desired state
gitops.description: The pipeline built and pushed pizza:3f9c2a1. How does the cluster find out? With kubectl in CI, the pipeline needs a production key. With GitOps, it only…
gitops.html:
The problem
The pipeline built and pushed pizza:3f9c2a1. How does the cluster find out? With kubectl in CI, the pipeline needs a production key. With GitOps, it only edits a file in git.
The big idea
Argo CD runs inside the cluster and watches a folder in git. When the folder changes, Argo CD applies it. When the cluster drifts from git, Argo CD puts it back. Git is the only way to change what runs.
📄 argocd/application.yaml
# Tells Argo CD: keep the pizza namespace matching deploy/ on the main branch.
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: pizza
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/OWNER/REPO.git # the hands-on lesson fills this in
    targetRevision: main
    path: deploy
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: pizza
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true # delete things removed from git
      selfHeal: true # undo changes made outside git
    syncOptions:
      - CreateNamespace=true
StatusMeaning
SyncedThe cluster matches git.
OutOfSyncGit and the cluster differ; Argo CD will sync if automated sync is on.
Healthy / Progressing / DegradedWhether the synced resources actually work, for example whether pods are ready.

Argo CD checks git about every 3 minutes by default. A webhook from GitHub can make it react within seconds.

Practice safely in the browser

Think of it like…
A thermostat. You set the temperature (git); the thermostat (Argo CD) keeps checking the room (the cluster) and heats or cools until they match.
Remember
  • Argo CD pulls from git and applies what it finds.
  • Synced = cluster matches git; Healthy = it actually works.
  • To change production, change git.

quiz.q: CI pushed a new tag to deploy/kustomization.yaml. What deploys it?
options: Argo CD, after it notices the change in git
quiz.why: Argo CD watches git and applies the change.

quiz.q: An app is Synced but Degraded. What does that mean?
options: The cluster matches git, but the app is not working
quiz.why: Sync status and health are separate questions.

repos.title: App repository and config repository
repos.description: Code and deployment settings change for different reasons, at different speeds, often by different people. Layout How it works Good for One repository (this…
repos.html:
Code and deployment settings change for different reasons, at different speeds, often by different people.

LayoutHow it worksGood for
One repository (this course)app/ and deploy/ live together; CI commits new tags into deploy/Learning, small teams
App repo + config repoCI in the app repo opens a commit or pull request in a separate config repoMany services, separate permissions, many environments
📄 deploy/kustomization.yaml
# Argo CD renders this folder. CI changes only the two image lines below.
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
namespace: pizza
resources:
  - deployment.yaml
  - service.yaml
images:
  - name: pizza
    newName: ghcr.io/owner/repo
    newTag: not-built-yet
The big idea
Promotion is a commit. Moving version 3f9c2a1 from staging to production means changing one line in production’s folder, reviewed like any other change.

No infinite loops: commits pushed with the workflow’s GITHUB_TOKEN do not start new workflow runs, and paths-ignore skips builds for commits that only change deploy/.

Remember
  • Code and deployment settings can live together or apart.
  • Promotion between environments is a reviewed commit.
  • A deploy-only commit should not trigger a rebuild.

quiz.q: How do you promote an already-tested image from staging to production with GitOps?
options: Commit its tag to production’s config
Rebuild it on a production server
quiz.why: Promotion reuses the exact same image; only git changes.

quiz.q: Why separate app and config repositories in bigger teams?
quiz.why: Separate repos let you control who can change production independently.

drift.title: Drift and self-heal
drift.description: During an incident someone runs kubectl scale --replicas=5 on production. It helps. Nobody writes it down. Next week a deploy quietly puts it back to 2 and…
drift.html:
The problem
During an incident someone runs kubectl scale --replicas=5 on production. It helps. Nobody writes it down. Next week a deploy quietly puts it back to 2 and the incident returns.
The big idea
With selfHeal on, Argo CD notices any difference between the cluster and git within seconds or minutes, and undoes it. Manual changes do not last; changes in git do.
kubectl -n pizza scale deploy/pizza --replicas=5   # a hand-made change
kubectl -n argocd get application pizza             # OutOfSync for a moment
kubectl -n pizza get deploy pizza                   # back to 2: git wins

Need the change to stay? Make it in git: change replicas in deploy/, commit, and push. During a real emergency, you can pause automated sync, but write the change into git before turning it back on.

Practice safely in the browser

Without selfHeal, Argo CD only shows OutOfSync and waits. With prune, it also deletes resources you removed from git. Know which options your apps use.
Remember
  • Drift = the cluster differs from git.
  • selfHeal undoes hand-made changes; prune removes deleted resources.
  • Lasting changes go through git.

quiz.q: selfHeal is on. Someone scales the app by hand from 2 to 5. What happens?
options: Argo CD returns it to 2, as git says
quiz.why: The cluster is brought back to the desired state in git.

quiz.q: You really need 5 copies. What is the GitOps way?
options: Change replicas in git and push
quiz.why: Changes in git are permanent and reviewed.

rollback.title: Roll back with git revert
rollback.description: Version two is live and customers report a bug. You need the old version back now, and you want a record of what happened. A deploy was a commit, so a…
rollback.html:
The problem
Version two is live and customers report a bug. You need the old version back now, and you want a record of what happened.
The big idea
A deploy was a commit, so a rollback is a commit too. git revert the deploy commit and push: Argo CD deploys the previous image. Nothing is rebuilt, and history shows who rolled back and when.
git log --oneline -- deploy/                   # find the deploy commit
git revert --no-edit <deploy-commit>
git push                                       # Argo CD deploys the previous tag
OptionSpeedWhen
Revert the deploy commitFast: the old image already existsThe newest release is bad and you need the last good one
Revert the code commitSlower: CI builds a new imageYou want the fix to go through the full pipeline

When a sync fails: look at the Application’s events and the pods. Common causes are a wrong image name (ImagePullBackOff), a private registry without a pull secret, or invalid YAML. Fix it in git; Argo CD retries.

Remember
  • Rollback = git revert of the deploy commit, then push.
  • No rebuild is needed: the previous image is still in the registry.
  • Fix failed syncs in git, not in the cluster.

quiz.q: Why is reverting the deploy commit fast?
options: The previous image is already built and stored
quiz.why: Only one line in git changes; the image already exists.

quiz.q: Pods show ImagePullBackOff after a sync. A likely cause?
options: The image name is wrong, or the registry is private
quiz.why: If tests had failed, nothing would have been promoted.

team.title: Team rules: protected branches, checks, approvals
team.description: Someone pushes straight to main at 6 p.m. without a review. The pipeline is green because there are no tests for the part they changed. Production breaks.…
team.html:
The problem
Someone pushes straight to main at 6 p.m. without a review. The pipeline is green because there are no tests for the part they changed. Production breaks.
The big idea
Make the safe path the only path: changes go through pull requests, required checks must pass, someone else approves, and production deploys need an extra approval.
RuleWhereStops
Require a pull request and one approvalRepository rules for mainUnreviewed changes
Require the test check to passRepository rulesMerging red builds
Block force pushesRepository rulesRewriting shared history
Environment with required reviewersSettings → EnvironmentsReleasing to production without a second person
CODEOWNERS for deploy/A CODEOWNERS fileProduction changes without the right reviewer

Keep pipelines fast. If CI takes 40 minutes, people find ways around it. Cache dependencies, run independent jobs in parallel, and keep slow tests for a nightly run.

Remember
  • Protect main: pull requests, required checks, no force pushes.
  • Use environments with reviewers for production.
  • A fast pipeline is a pipeline people actually use.

quiz.q: Which setting stops anyone merging when the test job is red?
options: A required status check on main
quiz.why: Required checks block the merge button until they pass.

quiz.q: Why keep CI fast?
options: Slow pipelines tempt people to skip them
quiz.why: A pipeline that everyone uses beats a perfect one everyone avoids.

real.title: Run the whole loop yourself
real.description: Now the real thing: your own public GitHub repository, a real pipeline, and Argo CD in a local kind cluster. It is free for public repositories. Keep Docker…
real.html:
Now the real thing: your own public GitHub repository, a real pipeline, and Argo CD in a local kind cluster. It is free for public repositories. Keep Docker running.

brew install kind kubectl gh
gh auth login
docker info --format "Docker {{.ServerVersion}} is running"
kind create cluster --name gitops
kubectl config current-context   # must print kind-gitops
kubectl create namespace argocd
kubectl apply -n argocd --server-side --force-conflicts -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/argoproj/argo-cd/stable/manifests/install.yaml
kubectl -n argocd rollout status deploy/argocd-server --timeout=5m

Stop if the context is anything other than kind-gitops, such as a work or production cluster. Switch with kubectl config use-context kind-gitops first.

Open Example files at the top of this page and choose Download all files (.zip). The next step expects gitops-examples.zip in your Downloads folder.

cd ~/Downloads && unzip -o gitops-examples.zip && mv gitops ~/pizza-gitops && cd ~/pizza-gitops
sed -i.bak "s|OWNER/REPO|$(gh api user -q .login)/pizza-gitops|" argocd/application.yaml && rm argocd/application.yaml.bak
git init -b main && git add -A && git commit -m "Pizza Express"
gh repo create pizza-gitops --public --source=. --push
gh run watch
git pull
cat deploy/kustomization.yaml

After it turns green, deploy/kustomization.yaml has your image name and a commit SHA. On GitHub, open your profile → Packages → pizza-gitops. If it says Private, use Package settings → Change visibility → Public so the cluster can download it.

kubectl apply -f argocd/application.yaml
kubectl -n argocd get application pizza
kubectl -n pizza rollout status deploy/pizza --timeout=5m
kubectl -n pizza run curl --rm -i --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl:8.11.1 -- curl -s pizza/

The answer shows the menu and version: the commit SHA that built the running image.

git pull --rebase
sed -i.bak 's/"Funghi"]/"Funghi", "Hawaiian"]/' app/app.py && rm app/app.py.bak
git commit -am "Add Hawaiian" && git push
gh run watch
kubectl -n argocd annotate application pizza argocd.argoproj.io/refresh=normal --overwrite
kubectl -n pizza rollout status deploy/pizza --timeout=5m
kubectl -n pizza run curl --rm -i --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl:8.11.1 -- curl -s pizza/

The annotate command asks Argo CD to check git now instead of within the next 3 minutes.

git pull --rebase
sed -i.bak 's/"Margherita", //' app/app.py && rm app/app.py.bak
git commit -am "Remove Margherita" && git push
gh run watch
git revert --no-edit HEAD && git push

The test job fails and build, scan, push, and promote are skipped; the cluster keeps running. The revert puts the test back to green.

kubectl -n pizza scale deploy/pizza --replicas=5
kubectl -n pizza get deploy pizza
sleep 20 && kubectl -n pizza get deploy pizza
gh run watch   # let the pipeline from the last step finish first
git pull --rebase
git log --oneline -3 -- deploy/
git revert --no-edit $(git log -1 --format=%H -- deploy/kustomization.yaml) && git push
kubectl -n argocd annotate application pizza argocd.argoproj.io/refresh=normal --overwrite
kubectl -n pizza rollout status deploy/pizza --timeout=5m

The revert only changes deploy/, so no new build runs: Argo CD deploys the previous image.

kind delete cluster --name gitops

Keep the repository as a portfolio project, or delete it on GitHub under Settings → Delete this repository.
